verdicts.reason: Naming a real identifiable instance as evidence is not the same as building an analogical transfer argument from a comparator program, and a comment can do either without the other.
Proposing measurement and feedback machinery is a different act from analyzing failure modes and edge conditions.
Spotting two cases the rule wrongly lumps together is internal to the rule, while reconciling against other named rules or dockets requires external regulatory references.
One requires quantities that carry the argument (possibly from the commenter's own records), the other requires locatable external source citations that need not be numeric.
A comment can supply a precise threshold or replacement wording without ever identifying the exact provision it targets, so precision of the ask and rule-text targeting can diverge.
Both score step-by-step tracing from the proposal to concrete consequences with identical zero anchors of bare assertion.
Rebutting an objection to one's own position is distinct from supplying a substitute policy approach; a comment can do either alone.
The alternative criterion demands an explained causal mechanism, whereas the precision criterion is satisfied by an exact ask with no mechanism at all.
The perverse-outcome criterion requires the effect to be opposed to the rule's stated purpose, a restriction the general causal-chain criterion does not impose.
Pinpointing and explaining proposed provisions is not the same as applying governing statutory or precedential language to the proposal.
Both reward a specified multi-step mechanism from rule to outcome and both zero out on unlinked assertion; the wording differs, not the concept.
Countering the agency's stated rationale is argumentative engagement, while adding information absent from the record is an evidentiary contribution.
Describing how the rule as proposed would be executed differs from proposing a different design that preserves the objective.
Proposing future data collection and validation is prospective, while integrating existing numbers into an argument is evidentiary.
One explicitly counts professional or secondhand expertise as qualifying depth, the other requires the commenter's own first-hand performance of the activity.
Designing monitoring and verification is not the same as quantifying effects against a baseline.
Weighing competing objectives is distinct from supplying an alternative approach; a tradeoff discussion need not propose anything.
One requires the experience to be tied to a cited provision or legal standard, a linkage the pure first-hand-experience criterion does not require.
Both score identification of specific affected groups plus the mechanism of asymmetric cost or benefit incidence; the difference is only granularity of the top anchor.
The second requires an explained causal mechanism for why the alternative works better, which the first does not demand.
Correcting an error or ambiguity in quoted rule language is diagnostic, while precision of the requested action is about the specificity of the ask.
Both reward connecting the proposal to governing statutory, delegated, or precedential language and both zero out on bare legal conclusions.
Both require personal experience tightly connected to a specific provision or regulatory mechanism rather than experience as color.
Steelmanning the strongest contrary rationale is a higher and distinct bar than acknowledging and responding to any one objection, so scores separate on weak-objection comments.
One rewards identifying barriers that block implementation, the other rewards laying out a workable implementation path; a comment can do one without the other.
Both require naming specific other regulatory instruments and reasoning about consistency or tension with the proposal.
Distributional equity is about who bears costs and benefits, while edge-case coverage is about contexts in which the rule operates differently.
Both score identification of interactions, conflicts, or duplication between the proposal and other rules or systems.
Anticipating a future risk the rule ignores need not involve textual ambiguity, and a textual ambiguity in a present situation need not be forward-looking.
Both reward analysis of timing, sequencing, phase-in, or seasonality connected to the rule's effects.
A developed excess-of-authority argument and the mechanical presence of part-and-section CFR citations are unrelated dimensions.
Pinpointing a proposed provision and requesting a revision is not legal-textual application of governing law.
The cascading criterion requires effects beyond the rule's intended scope and at least three links, while the general chain criterion accepts a chain to the intended outcome.
Calibrated partial agreement is about separating what is accepted from what is disputed, not about naming a provision and a revision.
One requires laying out two divergent readings and their consequences, the other covers any quoted error or misstatement corrected, including non-ambiguity errors.
Proposing a superior alternative with a mechanism is not the same as explaining the actors, resources, and timing of implementing the rule.
Rule-specific numeric content and precision of the requested change are separable; a comment can have exact numbers with no ask, or an exact ask with no numbers.
Answering the strongest contrary rationale on its own terms differs from comparing competing objectives and justifying a balance; a tradeoff analysis need not engage any opposing argument.
Offering an alternative design and proposing monitoring or verification machinery are unrelated contributions.
Proposing a workable alternative is distinct from recognizing and balancing competing objectives.
Both require a specific implementable alternative plus an explanation of how it still serves the agency's objective or works better.
Adding information absent from the record is the opposite pole from arguing off the agency's own preamble, figures, and cited studies.
Both score concrete observations from personal or local settings translated into a generalizable, rule-relevant implication, with anecdote alone as zero.
Tracing the proposal's own consequence chain is not the same as proposing an alternative rule with a mechanism.
A conflated internal distinction is not a cross-rule interaction or coordination problem.
Naming a provision and a revision is drafting-level specificity, not legal-authority analysis.
A missed distinction within the rule is internal, while conflict with another named statute or decision is external.
Explaining the rule's own behavioral causal chain differs from proposing an alternative rule with its own mechanism.
Both reward identifying the governing legal provision and applying it to the proposal with an explicit reasoning chain rather than bare citation.
Self-containment of the argument in the comment text and the presence of locatable external citations are near-orthogonal, arguably in tension.
Interpreting existing numbers is evidentiary, while proposing indicators and reporting triggers is prospective design.
The composite criterion additionally requires the fact to be first-hand and to carry an explicit consequence for an agency decision, neither of which the novelty criterion demands.
Cascading spillovers beyond intended scope are not necessarily outcomes diametrically opposed to the rule's stated purpose.
Naming a provision and a revision is different from showing that the rule conflates two materially different cases.
Naming what the proposal fails to say is gap analysis, whereas pinpointing engages what the proposal does say and asks for a revision.
Failure modes, secondary effects, and safeguards are a broader and different target than heterogeneity across contexts and affected populations.
Identifying implementation barriers is diagnostic, while proposing an alternative with a mechanism is prescriptive.
The rebuttal criterion is restricted to the agency's own NPRM reasoning, whereas counterargument engagement covers any objection from any source.
Both score whether the requested action is precise enough for a drafter to act on, with vague support or opposition as zero.
An unaddressed scenario in the rule's own text is not a comparison against other named rules or dockets.
Offering an alternative is a constructive act, while stating and answering the strongest contrary rationale is a dialectical one.
Pinpointing plus a proposed revision does not require alleging any error or ambiguity in the quoted language, which the correction criterion demands.
Both reward separating established fact from inference and assumption and calibrating stated confidence, penalizing false certainty.
Both score whether the comment supplies exact replacement language, thresholds, or parameters instead of a directional preference.
One targets the operative rule wording and its errors, the other targets the agency's stated rationale, impact figures, and cited studies, which may be engaged supportively.
A plain mechanism from proposal to consequence need not describe a perverse outcome contrary to the rule's purpose.
Numbers can be woven into a coherent analytical argument at a general policy level without being tied to how the specific provision under review operates.
Rebutting a named objection is distinct from explicitly weighing benefits, costs, and risks against one another.
A perverse-consequence argument is critical, while an alternative with a stated mechanism is constructive.
Rule-specific numbers and comparison against other named rules or dockets are unrelated dimensions.
Anticipating a future unaddressed problem does not require a documented real-world case contradicting a premise the rule rests on.
The omission criterion covers undelivered commitments and unassigned responsibilities generally, not only concrete scenarios the rule text fails to resolve.
Describing actors, workflows, and dependencies can be satisfied without alleging that any actor is unprepared or under-resourced, which the gap criterion requires.
Draftable operative parameters can be supplied with no causal account of why the alternative works better, and vice versa.
The cascading criterion imposes a minimum of three links and effects beyond the rule's intended scope, which the general mechanism criterion does not.
Targeting a provision for revision is unrelated to identifying conflicts or duplication across rules and agencies.
Both score a specific, checkable real-world instance that contradicts a premise the proposal depends on.
Naming a specific place or facility where impact lands is not the same as tracing who wins and who loses across distinct groups.
Both score whether the commenter supplies its own numeric compliance-cost estimate with a stated basis, with no figures as zero.
Rule-specific numbers and identification of a provision with a proposed revision are separable dimensions.
The cascading criterion requires spillover beyond intended scope with at least three links, a stricter and different target than a credible step-by-step mechanism.
One additionally penalizes unsourced round numbers and rewards verifiability, the other only asks that figures be tied to the provision's mechanics.
Both measure whether the agency ask is precise and actionable enough to be implemented directly, with generic support or opposition as zero.
Correcting the proposal's own wording is internal, while reconciling against other named rules or dockets is external.
The sourced-and-checkable criterion caps unsourced numbers at the midpoint, so analytically integrated but unsourced figures score high on one and mid on the other.
Laying out a workable implementation pathway differs from alleging that specific actors or systems are unprepared to carry out their role.
Both reward naming specific actors, systems, or processes that cannot deliver what the rule assumes, with the operational consequence explained.
Both score whether the legal argument correctly identifies the governing authority and reasons from it to the proposal rather than asserting a conclusion.
Both reward proposals for measurable data collection, testing, monitoring, or validation tied to revisiting the decision.
Reasoning about consistency includes showing harmony or redundancy, while the conflict criterion scores only when a concrete inconsistency is identified.
The baseline criterion specifically demands comparison against a baseline, alternative, or historical level, which analytically integrated numbers need not include.
Both reward an implementable alternative that still serves the proposal's legitimate objective, with bare rejection as zero.
The perverse-outcome requirement narrows one criterion to effects contrary to the rule's stated purpose; the general mechanism criterion accepts any traced consequence.
Group-level incidence of costs and benefits is distinct from tying an impact to a specific named place or institution.
A named real precedent used as supporting evidence need not cut against any premise the agency relies on, which the disconfirming-instance criterion requires.
Both score identification of specific affected populations with the mechanism of unequal cost or benefit exposure, penalizing undifferentiated appeals to the public.
Spillovers across systems and jurisdictions are a cross-sectional target, while long-horizon dynamics and adaptation are a temporal one.
A flawed definition or category boundary is not the same as a concrete scenario left unresolved by the rule text.
A missing commitment or unanswered question in the proposal is not necessarily an unprepared actor or system incapable of executing the rule.
The blind-spot criterion additionally requires surfacing a factual dynamic the agency appears unaware of, which pure first-hand experience does not.
Argument density relative to background is a compositional property, while legal reasoning quality is a substantive doctrinal one.
Both reward explicit comparison of competing benefits, costs, and objectives instead of one-sided advocacy.
Handling tradeoffs is about opposing considerations, while scope prioritization is about focus, ranking, and decision-readiness.
Focus and ranking of recommendations is unrelated to identifying an unanticipated future problem.
The cascading criterion requires at least three links and effects beyond intended scope, while the behavioral-mechanism criterion accepts any specified chain including a short one.
Both require named groups plus the mechanism of differential benefit or harm, with generic stakeholder language as zero.
Self-containment concerns whether substance lives in the text rather than attachments, while density concerns the ratio of argument to background within the text.
Comparing competing objectives and justifying a balance is a broader demand than identifying one objection and answering it, so a pure rebuttal and a pure balancing comment score differently.
One requires anchoring experience to cited regulatory text, the other requires surfacing an operational dynamic the agency has missed; neither entails the other.
Both score identification of specific groups bearing distinct costs or benefits with the mechanism of unequal incidence explained.
Conceding a real limitation of one's own position is not the same as identifying and rebutting an opposing argument.
Making a precise actionable request is unrelated to anticipating a problem the rule does not address.
Proposing an alternative rule is different from tracing the proposed rule's own mechanism to its consequences.
Both score whether claims rest on identifiable studies, records, or measurements relevant to the proposal, with bare assertion as zero.
An unprepared actor or system is one specific kind of problem; the anticipation criterion covers any unaddressed future risk, including non-implementation ones.
One rewards a clean account of who acts, with what resources and timing, the other requires showing precisely where the proposal breaks against an existing workflow.
A specified behavioral causal chain need not describe an outcome contrary to the rule's stated purpose.
Both reward a multi-step specified sequence from the proposal to a concrete consequence, with unlinked assertion as zero.
First-hand operational description and intensity of expressed feeling are unrelated and often inversely present.
The design-critique criterion additionally requires diagnosing a structural flaw in the regulation's architecture, which a draftable alternative alone does not supply.
Describing actors, workflows, and dependencies can conclude that the rule is workable, whereas the feasibility-analysis criterion scores only identified barriers.
Naming a provision and proposing a revision is not the same as showing that a concrete scenario is left unresolved by the text.
An unaddressed scenario is a silence in the rule, while a conflated distinction is an over-inclusive treatment of cases the rule does address.
The draftable-alternative criterion demands filled-in operative parameters, a stricter bar than proposing an alternative approach alongside an objection.
Correcting an error in what the proposal says is distinct from naming what the proposal fails to say or commit to.
Both reward a specified step-by-step chain from the proposal through behavior or implementation to consequences, with bare assertion as zero.
A definition can be ambiguous or circular without conflating two identifiable sub-cases, so the definitional criterion is broader than the conflation one.
Self-containment of the argument and the presence of analytically integrated numbers are unrelated dimensions.
Both require naming which groups gain or lose plus the concrete mechanism of the differential, penalizing generic public-interest language.
One requires explaining how the alternative preserves the objective, the other requires operative parameters concrete enough to draft; a comment can satisfy either alone.
Proposing monitoring and verification is unrelated to naming a provision and specifying a revision.
Whether substance lives in the comment text is orthogonal to whether the legal argument is doctrinally sound.
Both score concrete engagement with the actors, workflows, systems, and failure points that determine whether compliance can actually be executed.
The linkage criterion requires the experience to bear on how a specific regulatory mechanism operates, which raw first-hand operational detail does not.
Both score whether the comment situates the proposal against other rules and identifies interaction, conflict, or duplication rather than treating it in isolation.
Quantifying effects against a baseline is unrelated to tracing second-order spillovers across connected systems.
Engaging the preamble's reasoning or figures can be supportive or neutral, while the rebuttal criterion scores only when that reasoning is directly countered.
A precise ask can be made without identifying the exact provision it modifies, so precision and rule-text targeting can diverge.
One requires citation to a specific provision or legal standard, the other requires a record-absent fact plus a stated decision consequence, and neither entails the other.
Both score identification of which populations bear distinct costs or benefits together with the concrete exposure mechanism.
Pinpointing and explaining multiple provisions is unrelated to supplying rule-specific numeric figures.
The procedural criterion scores zero when there is no procedural dimension, so a precise substantive text request scores high on one and zero on the other.
Cross-rule consistency analysis and monitoring or verification design are unrelated contributions.
A flawed definition or category is a defect in what the rule says, while an omission is a defect in what it fails to say.
Both reward specific numbers that do argumentative work for the policy position rather than decorative figures, with purely qualitative text as zero.
The strongest-contrary criterion also credits answering another commenter's or the obvious objection, while the rebuttal criterion is restricted to the agency's stated rationale.
Both reward naming the responsible actors, systems, resources, and process conditions on which the rule's practical operation depends.
Both reward a specified step-by-step causal mechanism from the requirement to concrete effects, with bare assertion of harm or benefit as zero.
A concrete personal stake need not be tied to any cited provision or legal standard, which the anchored criterion requires.
The design-critique criterion requires diagnosing a structural flaw in the regulation's architecture in addition to offering the alternative.
Both require an explicitly linked multi-step causal chain from the rule to its claimed consequence rather than an unexplained assertion.
Both score whether a concrete alternative regulatory design is described specifically enough to be implemented, with mere objection as zero.
One rewards explaining how multiple provisions operate, the other requires specifying a concrete revision, so an explanatory comment with no proposed change diverges.
Explaining how provisions operate does not require alleging an error, ambiguity, or misstatement in the quoted language.
Both score detailed operational knowledge used to expose realities the rule fails to account for, differing mainly in wording about the knowledge's source.
